content.text:
The best long-term fix is **one resolver, and fail closed on an explicit provider prefix** — and I can now point at exactly why, because I verified the structure.

The same question ("which provider serves this model, and can it?") is answered **twice, by two paths with opposite failure semantics**:

```
gateway/index.ts:692  effectiveModel = resolveDispatchModel(...).model   ← checks routability, FAILS CLOSED
gateway/index.ts:703  resolveProviderConfig(agentId, effectiveModel, …)  ← re-derives the provider, FALLS OPEN
```

`resolveDispatchModel` even documents itself as "the SINGLE, shared dispatch-model resolver used by BOTH the enqueue gate and session-context, so they always agree." It hands `resolveProviderConfig` a model it has already certified routable — and `resolveProviderConfig` throws that decision away, re-derives the provider from the model *string*, and when it can't match, silently substitutes "first credentialed provider" while keeping the original model name. That substitution is what converts a precise fact ("gemini has no usable credential") into an opaque lie from a different vendor ("openai: 400 invalid model ID").

That divergence is the actual defect. Whichever of the two checks disagreed on gemini, the *disagreement itself* is what made the failure unreadable.

**So the fix, in order of leverage:**

1. **Make `resolveProviderConfig` consume the resolver's decision — the provider module — instead of re-deriving it.** One answer, computed once. This is the chokepoint that already serializes the choice, so it needs no new mechanism (your `AGENTS.md` "coordination design brake" says exactly this).

2. **Scope the fallback to unprefixed models only.** A bare `gpt-4o` legitimately needs a provider chosen for it. `gemini/gemini-2.5-pro` names its provider — if that provider can't serve it, the turn should fail with "gemini is not configured for this org", not get rerouted. This alone kills the entire class regardless of cause: missing capabilities block, undecryptable key, deleted row, revoked lease, expired OAuth. Your fail-closed invariant already mandates it for dispatch state; routing is the one place still fail-open.

3. **Make row validity explicit at rest.** `inference_providers` already has unused `status` and `error_message` columns. Recompute on every write: no modality block, or no decryptable key → `status='needs_configuration'` + reason, surfaced in the UI list and `lobu providers list`. That turns a silently dead row into a visible one, and a one-off recompute repairs every pre-existing row — which my create-time seed does *not* cover.

**What I'd avoid:** a DB `CHECK` that `capabilities` contains a text model — image/stt-only providers are legitimate, so it would be wrong as often as right. And more seeding at more call sites is whack-a-mole; #2316's seed is worth keeping as ergonomics, not as the guarantee.

Sequencing: (2) is the small, high-value one and is independently shippable. (1) is the real consolidation and is where I'd put the effort. (3) is what makes the problem visible to you instead of to me at 3am.

One honest caveat: I have not yet traced *why* the two checks disagreed on gemini specifically — `resolveDispatchModel` considered it routable (it passed the model through unchanged) while `findProviderForModel` did not match it. My leading suspect is `getModelOptions` throwing during credential resolution inside the match loop. That question only matters for (1); (2) and (3) are correct regardless.

PR #2316 is still with `make review`; I'll report the verdict and CI, and merge if green.

## 🚨 An ALIAS slug (slug !== kind) needs `base_url` or it CANNOT route
`getModelPolicy` keys its module map by the row's **SLUG**, not its `kind`. So:
- `slug === kind` (e.g. `gemini`/`gemini`) → the catalog's STATIC module answers → routes with

- `slug !== kind` (e.g. `my-gemini`/`gemini`) → no static module under that id → the ONLY path

  it the row is dropped by the policy no matter what else is set.

Consequence that makes it dangerous: a text model is also the predicate
`promoteOldestRunnableProvider` uses to pick the org default
(`capabilities #>> '{text,model}' IS NOT NULL`). So giving an unroutable alias row a model
PROMOTES it to org default and breaks every allow-all agent in the org. Caught by `make
review` as a blocker on #2316's first revision — a real find, verified before acting.

content.text:
`make review` caught a **real blocker** on #2316, and it's worth reporting because it reinforces the answer I gave you.

**The finding (verified, not taken on trust):** `getModelPolicy` keys its module map by the row's **slug**, not its `kind`. So `slug === kind` (`gemini`/`gemini`) resolves via the catalog's static module and routes with just a text model. But an **alias** (`slug=my-gemini, kind=gemini`) has no static module under that id, so its only path is synthesis — which requires `base_url`. My seed gave such a row a text model, and a text model is exactly the predicate `promoteOldestRunnableProvider` uses to pick the org default. Net effect: an unroutable row would have been **promoted to org default**, breaking every allow-all agent in the org.

Fixed: seed only when the row will actually route (`slug === kind`, or a `base_url` is present), and log why when it won't. Two new tests pin it — the alias row must be unseeded *and* `is_default = false`. Mutation-tested: removing the guard fails exactly that test. 6/6 green, 24 regression tests pass, `make pre-pr` clean. Pushed; review is re-running.

I also hit the fixer-pass trap: I edited files while `make review-fix` was still writing, and its final write silently dropped my `logger.warn`. I only caught it because the blocker fix made me re-read. Re-applied and verified by reading back.

**This is direct evidence for the long-term fix.** The blocker exists because "which provider serves this slug?" is answered by *slug* in the module map, by *kind* in the catalog gate, and by *string prefix* in `findProviderForModel` — three answers to one question, in one request path. That's the same divergence as the fail-closed/fail-open split between `resolveDispatchModel` and `resolveProviderConfig`. Consolidating to one resolver isn't cosmetic; it's what stops this class of bug from regenerating every time someone touches the area. My PR is a guardrail around the symptom, not the cure.

Confidence: **85** on #2316 now — the blocker is fixed and mutation-tested, but the reviewer also flagged `tests_adequate: false` and wanted a test proving the created row resolves to an actual *module* rather than just asserting stored capabilities. My `is_default` assertion covers the harmful consequence, not the resolution itself; a true policy-level test needs module registration in the test process.

Next: report the re-review verdict and CI, then merge if green. Then the consolidation work — I'd start with scoping the fallback to unprefixed models, since it's small, independently shippable, and turns every instance of this class into a named error.

Outstanding after this merges:
1. The consolidation I'd actually recommend — scope the fallback to unprefixed models so an explicit `gemini/…` fails with a named error instead of being rerouted. Small and independently shippable.
2. A repair pass for pre-existing blockless rows; the seed only covers creation, and I fixed your two by hand.

4. Your Behaviors still pin `z-ai/glm-5.2` and burn retries against a quota that resets 2026-07-31.
1 is the best long term you think?

No — and I should correct my own framing, because I blurred two different things.

Scoping the fallback is the best **first** step, not the best long-term fix. It's the smallest change that converts every instance of this class into a named error, and it's independently shippable. But it treats the symptom: it makes divergence *loud* instead of making divergence *impossible*.

The best long-term fix is the one I listed as the consolidation: **resolve provider identity once, and pass a resolved object instead of a string.**

Here's the case for it. Count how many places independently answer "which provider serves this model?" in a single turn:

| Layer | How it decides |
|---|---|
| `getModelPolicy` | slug → `moduleMap`, else org-row synthesis |
| catalog gate (create) | `kind` → catalog entry |
| `findProviderForModel` | exact model-option match, else **string prefix** |
| `resolveDispatchModel` | routability over modules (fails closed) |
| `resolveProviderConfig` | re-derives, then **falls open** to first credentialed |
| worker `resolveModelRef` | strips prefixes by comparing to `defaultProvider`/`defaultProviderSlug` |

Six derivations of one fact, from a stringly-typed `"gemini/gemini-2.5-pro"`, with different rules. Today's bug was #4 and #5 disagreeing. This week's blocker was #1 keying by *slug* while #2 keys by *kind*. Those aren't two bugs — they're the same bug twice, which is exactly the signal your `AGENTS.md` calls out ("same root cause twice = stop reviewing, grep-enumerate").

Replace it with one resolution at the boundary producing something like `{ providerModule, upstreamSlug, bareModelId, credentialSource }`, and every downstream consumer reads fields instead of re-parsing. Then the fallback stops being an implicit re-derivation and becomes one explicit, testable decision; the worker stops guessing at prefix-stripping; and adding a provider kind can't introduce a seventh interpretation. Notably, it also makes my open question — *why* `resolveDispatchModel` and `findProviderForModel` disagreed on gemini — permanently moot rather than something I still owe you an answer on.

**Why not do it first:** it touches the hottest path in the product, spans gateway + worker + catalog, and your own "coordination design brake" invariant warns against exactly that kind of big-bang change. Doing fail-closed first is what makes it safe — once nothing silently substitutes, any divergence introduced during the refactor shows up as a loud failure instead of a misroute you discover months later in a Telegram chat.

One thing I'd rank above both for *your* experience, though: the row-validity status (my #3). Fail-closed turns "no reply" into "error: gemini not configured" — still a failure you hit at message time. Validating at write and surfacing `needs_configuration` in the UI means the bad state never exists. It's narrower (it can't catch runtime causes like a revoked key or an exhausted quota), which is why it's a complement, not a replacement.

So the honest ordering: **fail-closed now** (small, general, unblocks the rest) → **single resolver** (the actual cure) → **row status** (prevention + the only one your users see). If you only ever do one, do the single resolver; if you only do one *this week*, do fail-closed.

Analysis 2026-07-29, after two bugs in one day that were the SAME root cause
(see [[reference_org_provider_needs_base_url]], [[project_agent_model_provider_resolution]]).

## The class
Provider identity travels as a stringly-typed ref (`"gemini/gemini-2.5-pro"`) and is
**re-derived independently at six layers in a single turn**, each with different rules:

| Layer | Decides by |
|---|---|
| `getModelPolicy` (provider-catalog.ts) | **slug** → `moduleMap`, else org-row synthesis |
| catalog gate on create (agent-routes.ts) | **kind** → catalog entry |
| `findProviderForModel` | exact model-option match, else **string prefix** |
| `resolveDispatchModel` | routability over modules — **fails CLOSED** |
| `resolveProviderConfig` (gateway/index.ts) | re-derives, then **falls OPEN** to first credentialed |
| worker `resolveModelRef` | strips prefix by comparing to `defaultProvider`/`defaultProviderSlug` |

Two bugs, same cause:
- gemini 400: layers 4 and 5 disagreed → silent substitution → `openai` got `gemini/gemini-2.5-pro`.
- #2316 review blocker: layer 1 keys by **slug**, layer 2 by **kind** → an alias row looked
  configured and would have been promoted to org default while being unroutable.

## Recommended order (cost/risk weighted)
1. **Fail closed on an explicit prefix.** If the ref names its provider and that provider
   can't serve it, error naming THAT provider; keep the fallback only for unprefixed refs.
   Small, general (covers every cause: missing block, bad key, deleted row, revoked lease,
   quota), independently shippable. Do this FIRST — it makes step 2 safe, because after it a
   divergence is a loud failure instead of a silent misroute.
2. **Resolve once; pass a typed object**, e.g.
   `{ providerModule, upstreamSlug, bareModelId, credentialSource }`. Downstream reads fields
   instead of re-parsing. This is THE cure — it makes a 7th interpretation unrepresentable and
   moots "why did layers 4 and 5 disagree" (never traced). Touches the hottest path
   (gateway + worker + catalog), so it is NOT a first move — cf. the repo's
   "Coordination design brake" invariant.
3. **Row validity at rest.** `inference_providers` already has UNUSED `status` +
   `error_message` columns. Recompute on write: no modality block, or alias slug without
   base_url, or undecryptable key → `status='needs_configuration'` + reason; surface in the UI
   list and `lobu providers list`. The only one a USER sees, and it prevents the bad state
   instead of diagnosing it — but it cannot cover runtime causes, so it complements (1).

**Do NOT** add a DB CHECK requiring `capabilities.text` — image/stt-only providers are
legitimate. And do not add more seeding at more call sites; that is whack-a-mole. #2316's
create-time seed is ergonomics, NOT the guarantee.
